slides.title: In 1880, Alexander Graham Bell made a wireless phone call.
slides.sub: He said it beat the telephone.

slides.kicker: A voice, with no wire at all.
slides.body:
In 1880, Bell and his assistant Charles Sumner Tainter were working in a lab on L Street, in Washington, D.C.

They wanted to send speech without a wire. Just on a beam of light.
The mirror made the sunlight flicker. Selenium turned that flicker back into electric current, and then into sound.

Tainter stood on the roof of a nearby school and spoke into the light. In the lab, Bell heard:

"Mr. Bell, if you understand what I say, come to the window and wave your hat."

Bell waved his hat.

slides.kicker: He loved it more than the telephone.
slides.body:
Bell called the photophone "the greatest invention I have ever made; greater than the telephone."

He even wanted to name his second daughter Photophone. His wife Mabel talked him out of it. They chose Marian.

slides.kicker: But one cloud could end the call.
slides.body:
The photophone needed sunshine and a clear, straight line of sight. Clouds, fog, rain and night all stopped it.

Radio came along instead, and the photophone was mostly forgotten.

slides.kicker: A century later, light came back.
slides.body:
Lasers and ultra-clear glass fibres solved the problems Bell couldn't.

Today, fibre-optic cables carry calls and internet data as pulses of light. The photophone is often called their ancestor.

slides.lead: Being early can look exactly like being wrong.
slides.accent: Sometimes a good idea is just waiting for its missing piece.

slides.line: Save this for the next time a good idea gets dismissed.

caption:
In 1880, Alexander Graham Bell and Charles Sumner Tainter sent a voice across Washington, D.C. on a beam of sunlight. They called it the photophone, and Bell said it was greater than the telephone. Clouds and darkness stopped it, but the same idea now runs through fibre-optic cables.

What's an idea you've seen that was right, just too early?
